title: The perfect aspect across tenses
tagline: Complete before now, before then, or before a point still to come — one logic, three timelines.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 1 — multiple-choice cloze (choosing the right tense and aspect)
Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations (FOR, SINCE, ALREADY, JUST, BY)
Writing Part 2 — report or review: sequencing events accurately
Speaking Part 2 — describing experience, change and progress over time
why: At C1, the perfect aspect stops being 'the present perfect tense' and becomes a tool you use across all three timelines to show that one event is complete before a reference point. Use & of English tests the fine line between simple and continuous forms directly, and examiners notice when a candidate can move fluently between has done, had done and will have done without defaulting to the simple past.

diagrams.caption: Whichever tense it borrows, the perfect aspect always looks back from a reference point to something already complete.

diagrams.title: Perfect infinitive and perfect -ing
diagrams.caption: The perfect infinitive points back after a modal or reporting verb; perfect -ing sequences two actions in a single sentence.

head: Pattern
Reference point
Example
rows: has revised all term / has been revising all week
had already left / had been waiting for an hour
will have graduated / will have been studying for six years
after a modal or reporting verb

use.point: Present perfect simple vs continuous: the result vs the activity

examples.text: Nadia has read the whole set text twice this term.
Nadia has been reading late into the night all week, and it shows.
examples.note: continuous: the activity, with visible present evidence

examples.text: I've lived in Cusco for six years, but I've only been living in this flat since March.
examples.note: a permanent state (simple) vs a recent, possibly temporary one (continuous)

use.point: Past perfect (simple and continuous) with before, by the time and until

examples.text: By the time the results were announced, Liam had already accepted a place at another school.
Her hands were shaking because she had been rehearsing the speech for hours.
examples.note: the activity leading up to the past moment

examples.text: Mateo hadn't finished the essay before the deadline passed.
examples.note: an unmet deadline, seen from a later point

use.point: Future perfect (simple and continuous) with by and by the time

examples.text: By next June, the school orchestra will have performed in four countries.
examples.note: a completed total by a future point

examples.text: By the time you read this, I will have left for the airport.
examples.note: future perfect seen from the reader's later perspective

examples.text: In September, Sofia will have been studying French for a decade.
examples.note: duration continuing up to a future point

use.point: Perfect infinitive and perfect -ing: pointing back to an earlier action

examples.text: The team seems to have solved the coding problem overnight.
examples.note: an inference about something that happened earlier

examples.text: Having submitted the coursework early, Nadia spent the weekend relaxing.
examples.note: one clearly finished action before another

watch_out.why: A finished time expression (yesterday) needs the past simple, not the present perfect.

watch_out.wrong: She has been living here since ten years.
watch_out.right: She has been living here for ten years.
watch_out.why: Since introduces a point in time; for introduces a duration.

watch_out.wrong: By the time we arrived, the film already started.
watch_out.right: By the time we arrived, the film had already started.
watch_out.why: An action completed before another past action needs the past perfect, not the past simple.

watch_out.wrong: I will have finish the report by Friday.
watch_out.right: I will have finished the report by Friday.
watch_out.why: Future perfect needs the past participle after have, not the bare infinitive.

watch_out.wrong: He claims to have win the competition twice.
watch_out.right: He claims to have won the competition twice.
watch_out.why: The perfect infinitive is to have + past participle, never to have + base form.

watch_out.wrong: She has been knowing the answer for ages.
watch_out.right: She has known the answer for ages.
watch_out.why: Stative verbs like know don't normally take the continuous, even in the perfect.

dialogue.title: One week before the mock exam
dialogue.context: Miss Vega checks how the class is preparing for Friday's mock exam, and the students report their progress using the perfect aspect.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Right, before Friday's mock — what exactly have you done this week?

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: I've finished the whole grammar workbook, and I've been revising vocabulary every evening.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Less, I'm afraid. By Sunday I'll have read only half the set novel.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Still a start. Sofia, what about the writing paper?

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: I'd already written two practice essays before half term, so this week I focused on speaking.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: I feel behind everyone else. I hadn't realised how much listening practice this exam needs until yesterday.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: That's exactly why we're doing this now, not the night before the exam.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: By the time the exam comes round, I hope I'll have covered every paper from the last five years.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Having seen Nadia's notes, I finally understand how much organisation matters.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: And once this term has finished, we can finally relax — for about a week.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Fair enough. Then you'll all have learnt something valuable even before the results arrive.

items.sentence: By the time the guests arrived, Mrs Alva ___ dinner.
items.why: an action completed before another past action needs the past perfect simple

items.sentence: ___ this novel? You must read it, it's brilliant.
items.why: an experience within an unfinished period (life) needs the present perfect

items.sentence: My eyes are sore because I ___ at a screen all afternoon.
items.why: a visible present result of a recent activity needs the present perfect continuous

items.sentence: ___ the marathon by six o'clock tomorrow.
items.why: completed before a specific future point needs the future perfect

items.sentence: The manager claims ___ the letter, but nobody received it.
items.why: an earlier action reported in the present needs the perfect infinitive

items.sentence: ___ the report, she went straight to bed.
items.why: perfect -ing shows one action completed just before another

items.sentence: He ___ the guitar since he was seven, so he's remarkably good now.
items.why: a long activity continuing up to now, with present relevance, favours the continuous

summary: The perfect aspect frames an event as complete before a reference point — now, a past moment or a future one.
Simple forms (has written) focus on the result; continuous forms (has been writing) focus on the activity and its visible effects.
By, by the time and before often signal a deadline that needs a perfect form, not the simple past or future.
After modals and reporting verbs, use the perfect infinitive (to have left); to sequence two past actions in one sentence, use perfect -ing (Having left).
Stative verbs (know, own, believe) rarely take the continuous, even in the perfect.
